newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada rate cut speculation rises on weak data.
newsitem.headline: Canada rate cut speculation rises on weak data.

text.p: A strengthening Canadian dollar and a weak retail sales report on Monday boosted speculation that the Bank of Canada will soon chop interest rates again.
Speculation about further rate cuts heightened after Canada's statistical agency reported that Canadian retail sales fell 0.4 percent in August.
Economists surveyed by Reuters had forecast sales would rise by 0.4 percent in the month.
Canadian money markets firmed on expectations of another rate easing. Some analysts said a cut may come as soon as Tuesday if a report on consumer prices shows lower-than-expected inflation.

"The flavor is coming back into the market that the bank will cut. I think that everybody believed that they would cut (again). It was just a matter of time," said John Johnston, an economist with Royal Bank of Canada.
Another interest rate cut by the Bank of Canada would bring rates in Canada, already at their lowest levels in almost 40 years, to near historic lows.

The central bank trimmed rates to their lowest levels in decades last week when it cut its key bank rate by 25 basis points to 3.75 percent. The bank rate is similar to the U.S. Federal Funds rate, the rate at which banks lend each other short-term funds. The U.S. rate now stands at 5.25 percent.
Last week's reduction was the ninth this year and the eighth independent of a move by the U.S. Federal Reserve.
The Bank of Canada has been steadily cutting Canadian interest rates since May 1995 in a bid to offset the negative impact of goverment spending cuts.
The retail sales report showed "surprising weakness" and confirmed that the domestic demand in Canada remains lackluster, said Royal Bank's Johnston.

"The key thing that's been missing in recent quarters is the Canadian consumer, and this morning's evidence from retail sales suggests they're still not participating at the party," said Dan Kelly, director of financial markets research with CIBC Wood Gundy Securities Inc.
The performance of Canada's currency is seen as the biggest factor governing the timing of another rate cut.

After its two most recent cuts, the central bank issued statements that the easings were done to offset the impact of a strengthening currency on the Canadian economy. A stronger dollar has the same effect as a hike in interest rates because it makes exports less competitive.

The Canadian dollar has strengthened more since the last easing on Oct. 16 and traded at about C$1.3474 to the U.S dollar Monday afternoon. Dealers said a rate cut becomes more likely as the currency strengthens toward C$1.3400 against the U.S. currency.
A report on consumer prices scheduled for release on Tuesday could also spur a rate cut, some analysts said.
Economists surveyed by Reuters forecast the consumer price index report for September will show inflation at about 1.4 percent, one of the lowest rates in the industrialized world.
